text: You already know a service principal is the identity an app uses. What's worth being precise about, right before this discipline moves onto AWS, is exactly what objects are involved and how their credentials work — because that's where most real compromises of non-human identities happen.

Every app registration creates two objects. The application object is the global definition — name, permissions, credential configuration. The service principal is the tenant-local identity that actually authenticates and holds RBAC assignments. In a multi-tenant app, one application object produces a separate service principal in every tenant that consents to it, and it's that service principal that shows up in sign-in logs and gets granted access.

A service principal authenticates with one of three credential types, and Microsoft's guidance pushes toward a specific order. Federated credentials let an external workload, like a GitHub Actions run, exchange its own OIDC token for an Entra ID token with no secret stored anywhere. Certificates come next — a private key is harder to leak than plain text. Client secrets are the last resort: easy to leak into source control or CI logs, and the most common root cause of a compromised service principal. If one is unavoidable, give it a short expiration and store it in Key Vault.

A managed identity removes the credential problem entirely — the platform rotates it behind the scenes, reachable only by the resource it's attached to, so your code never sees a secret. System-assigned identities are created and destroyed with the resource, one-to-one. User-assigned identities are standalone resources with their own lifecycle, attachable to multiple resources at once — useful when a fleet of instances all need the same identity without separate RBAC assignments for each.

Whether securing a service principal or a managed identity, the same RBAC discipline from the last lesson applies. A non-human identity should get the narrowest role at the narrowest scope its job requires — never Owner or Contributor on a subscription because figuring out the real scope felt like extra work. A managed identity that only reads secrets from one Key Vault should hold Key Vault Secrets User scoped to that vault, so a compromised workload is bounded by exactly what you scoped it to.

Application object versus service principal, credentials ranked from federated down to client secret as a last resort, system-assigned versus user-assigned identities, and RBAC scoped tightly enough to bound a compromise — that closes out Azure identity security. Chapter 3 moves this same discipline onto AWS's IAM model, where the concepts rhyme but the mechanics differ.
